title: Rising spirits, good for all
hook: every Ardas ends asking chardi kala through the Name and the good of all
tomorrow: Why the Gurus kept others' hymns

segments.voice: Yesterday, amal: deeds are the soil. Today, the last of the Granth's great themes, and the last line of every Ardas.

The program at the gurdwara is ending. The whole congregation stands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, hands folded. One person leads the Ardas, the standing prayer, remembering the Gurus, the martyrs, the sacrifices of centuries. It's long, and parts of it are heavy with history. Then it ends. Not with a request for our side to win, or for this group to prosper. It ends with a line that reaches past the door, past the city, to everyone alive. Today: sarbat da bhala.
screen: `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.` → `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS.` → `THEN, THE LAST LINE.`

segments.voice: The Ardas has grown over time. Its opening lines come from the Chandi di Var, which Sikh tradition attributes to Guru Gobind Singh, and later generations added the remembrance of the martyrs. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib, but Sikhs say it at gurdwaras, at home, before a journey, at weddings and funerals. It closes with these words: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Two phrases, each a whole teaching. Chardi kala means rising spirits: a spirit that keeps climbing, optimistic, unbroken, even in loss. And it's asked for through the Name, naam, not through luck or strength. Then: tere bhaane, by your will, sarbat da bhala. Sarbat means all, everyone, the whole. Bhala means good, well-being. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs, or of the ones who agree. Everyone. Consider where this is said. The Ardas remembers people who were persecuted and killed. You might expect a prayer like that to end in anger. It ends in the good of all. It also closes this part of the path, the Granth's great themes: hukam and haumai, naam and nadar, the thieves and the virtues, maya, the gurmukh, sahaj, the bride and her longing, the written date, the light in everyone, truth lived, deeds as soil. And it all opens out here: a spirit that rises, and a wish that includes everyone.
screen: `THE ARDAS — THE STANDING PRAYER.` · `CHARDI KALA — RISING SPIRITS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA — GOOD OF ALL.` · `IT ALL OPENS OUTWARD.` · then, large: `THE GOOD OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Start close: picture someone you love and wish them well, then someone you barely know, the neighbor, the driver, then someone difficult, someone you'd rather not think about, if only a little. Then widen it: the street, the city, everyone. If you pray, you can say the Ardas's last words, sarbat da bhala; or simply, in your own words, good for everyone.
Chardi kala, rising spirits, asked through the Name in the closing wish of every Ardas, alongside sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
Your line: the good of all. It's a wish that leaves no one out. That's day two hundred fifty-one.

what a scholar hears: the Ardas is not part of the Granth; its opening invocation is from the Chandi di Var in the Dasam Granth, traditionally attributed to Guru Gobind Singh (authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth is debated), later sections were added over time, and its form was set in the Sikh Rehat Maryada.
